props.title: Hurlyburly

sections.content: Hurlyburly (1998) stands as a searing adaptation of David Rabe's 1984 play, capturing Hollywood's cocaine-fueled excess through the lens of entertainment industry players spiraling through existential crises. Director Anthony Drazan maintains the theatrical intensity while opening up the claustrophobic setting, letting Sean Penn's manic performance as Eddie breathe in the Hollywood Hills. The film belongs to a specific late-90s wave of Hollywood self-examination, alongside Swimming with Sharks (1994) and The Player (1992), but dives deeper into psychological territory than its contemporaries.

sections.content: The film's exploration of toxic masculinity and emotional violence feels especially relevant today, though its theatrical roots sometimes show through in the dialogue's density. Penn's performance is matched by a stellar ensemble including Kevin Spacey, Chazz Palminteri, and Robin Wright, all handling Rabe's complex language with remarkable dexterity. Like American Buffalo (1996) and Tape (2001), the film demonstrates how stage-to-screen adaptations can maintain verbal intensity while finding a distinctly cinematic voice. SUBHEAD: Hollywood Self-Reflection

Hurlyburly fits into a larger tradition of Hollywood examining its own moral bankruptcy, though it focuses more on psychological deterioration than industry critique. While films like The Big Picture (1989) and Living in Oblivion (1995) tackle the mechanics of filmmaking, Hurlyburly uses the entertainment industry as a backdrop for exploring masculine crisis and spiritual emptiness. The film's cocaine-fueled paranoia echoes Less Than Zero (1987), another exploration of Los Angeles excess, but with a sharper existential edge.
